title: Buffered Channels & Direction
summary: A **buffered channel** `make(chan T, n)` holds up to `n` values, so sends succeed without a waiting receiver until the buffer is full. **Directional channel types** (`chan<- T` send-only, `<-chan T` receive-only) let function signatures document and enforce who produces and who consumes.

subtopics.title: Capacity vs length
subtopics.explanation: make(chan T, n) creates a channel whose buffer holds n values: cap(ch) is n and len(ch) is how many values are currently buffered (waiting to be received). They behave like a fixed-size FIFO queue between goroutines. This distinction is the mental model for everything a buffered channel does.

subtopics.title: When a buffered send blocks
subtopics.explanation: A send on a buffered channel succeeds immediately as long as the buffer has room; once the buffer is full, further sends block until a receiver frees a slot. So buffering decouples producer and consumer up to n outstanding items — the core benefit of adding a buffer.

subtopics.title: When a buffered receive blocks
subtopics.explanation: A receive returns a buffered value immediately if the buffer is non-empty; if it's empty, the receive blocks until a send arrives (or the channel is closed), and FIFO order is preserved. This is the mirror image of send blocking and completes the buffered-channel timing picture.

subtopics.title: Send-only direction chan<- T
subtopics.explanation: A parameter of type chan<- T may only be sent on, not received from; passing a bidirectional channel to such a parameter restricts its use, documenting that the function is a producer. Directional types encode the producer half of the data-flow contract in the type system.

subtopics.title: Receive-only direction <-chan T
subtopics.explanation: A parameter of type <-chan T may only be received from; it documents a consumer and prevents the function from sending or closing the channel by mistake. Paired with chan<- T, it makes each function's role in a pipeline unambiguous at compile time.

subtopics.title: Choosing a buffer size (decoupling)
subtopics.explanation: Use unbuffered for strict synchronization, a small buffer to absorb bursts or decouple timing, and a buffer sized to known work (e.g. the number of goroutines) so senders never block. Oversized buffers hide backpressure and can mask leaks. Sizing the buffer is how you tune the degree of decoupling between producer and consumer.

foundations.overview: Unbuffered channels force a sender to wait for a receiver. Often that's too strict — you want a producer to keep working while a consumer catches up, or you want to collect a known number of results without each send blocking. A buffered channel adds a fixed-size queue between the two, so sends succeed until the queue fills. Directional channel types are the other half of the story: they let a function's signature say 'I only send here' or 'I only receive here', which makes concurrent code self-documenting and catches misuse at compile time.
foundations.formalDefinition: A buffered channel is a channel with capacity n > 0 backed by an n-element FIFO ring buffer; sends block only when the buffer is full and receives block only when it is empty. A directional channel type (chan<- T or <-chan T) restricts a channel value to send-only or receive-only operations.
foundations.whyItMatters: Buffering is how you absorb bursts, decouple producer/consumer speeds, and size result channels so workers don't block. Directional types are everywhere in real pipeline and worker-pool APIs, encoding the data-flow contract in the type system — a frequent interview and code-review topic.
foundations.mentalModel: A buffered channel is a conveyor belt with n slots: the producer drops items on while there's room and only stops when the belt is full; the consumer picks them off the front in order. A directional type is a one-way sign on the belt: 'drop-off only' or 'pickup only'.
foundations.runtimePerspective: The runtime backs a buffered channel with a circular buffer plus the same lock and wait queues as an unbuffered one. A send copies into the buffer when there's room (no goroutine handoff needed); only when full does it park the sender. Directional types are purely a compile-time restriction — at runtime it's the same hchan.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Job queues sized to expected backlog, result channels sized to the number of workers, semaphore patterns (a buffered channel as a token bucket), and pipeline stages that need slack between them.
foundations.businessImpact: Right-sized buffers smooth out traffic spikes so a service degrades gracefully instead of blocking or dropping work, improving tail latency and reliability under load.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Directional types make APIs harder to misuse: a consumer literally cannot close or send on its input, eliminating a class of ownership bugs at compile time.
foundations.performanceImpact: A buffer reduces goroutine parking when producer and consumer rates differ, improving throughput. But an oversized buffer wastes memory and hides backpressure, letting problems accumulate silently.
commonUseCases: Result channels sized to the number of workers
Bounded job queues that absorb bursts
Counting semaphores (chan struct{} of size N)
APIs using chan<- / <-chan to enforce producer/consumer roles

commonMisconceptions.reality: It blocks on send when the buffer is full and on receive when it's empty — buffering only delays blocking by n items.

commonMisconceptions.myth: len(ch) and cap(ch) are the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: cap(ch) is the buffer size; len(ch) is how many values are currently buffered and waiting to be received.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Directional channel types are separate channels.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They're restricted views of the same channel; a bidirectional chan T converts implicitly to chan<- T or <-chan T, but not back.

config.intro: Behavior of make(chan int, 2), step by step:

steps.name: First send
steps.detail: ch <- 1 copies into slot 0; buffer has room, so the send returns immediately. len=1, cap=2.

steps.name: Second send
steps.detail: ch <- 2 copies into slot 1. Buffer now full. len=2, cap=2.

steps.name: Third send blocks
steps.detail: ch <- 3 finds the buffer full and parks the sender until a slot frees up.

steps.name: Receive frees a slot
steps.detail: <-ch returns 1 (FIFO). A slot opens, so the parked sender of 3 completes.

steps.name: Direction enforced
steps.detail: Passed as chan<- int, only sends compile; as <-chan int, only receives — the same buffer, restricted view.

interactiveExamples.title: Sends don't block until the buffer is full
interactiveExamples.explanation: With capacity 2, the first two sends succeed without any receiver. len(ch) tracks how many values are buffered. A third send (uncomment to see) would block forever here, causing a deadlock.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int, 2)   // buffer holds 2
	ch <- 10                  // ok, buffer has room
	ch <- 20                  // ok, buffer now full
	fmt.Println(len(ch), cap(ch)) // 2 2
	fmt.Println(<-ch)             // 10 (FIFO)
	fmt.Println(<-ch)             // 20
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: a counting semaphore with a buffered channel
interactiveExamples.explanation: A buffered channel of size n is a classic semaphore: acquiring sends a token (blocks when n are out), releasing receives one. Fill in acquire/release so at most 2 workers run concurrently. This pattern bounds concurrency without a mutex.

checkpoints.code:
ch := make(chan int, 3)
ch <- 1
ch <- 2
fmt.Println(len(ch), cap(ch))
checkpoints.explanation: cap(ch) is 3, the buffer size set by make. len(ch) is 2, the number of values currently buffered (sent but not yet received). Two sends into a size-3 buffer don't block.

options: The second send blocks on a full buffer with no receiver running
len must equal cap before receiving
Buffered channels must be closed first
checkpoints.explanation: The buffer holds 1. The first send fills it; the second send blocks waiting for a free slot. Since main is the only goroutine and it's stuck on that send, no one receives — the runtime reports a deadlock.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the effect of declaring a parameter as `<-chan int`?
options: The function can only send on it
The function can only receive from it
checkpoints.explanation: <-chan int is a receive-only channel type: inside the function you may receive (and range) but not send or close. It documents and enforces that the function is a consumer.

checkpoints.prompt: Size the results channel so N worker goroutines can each send once without ever blocking.
checkpoints.codeAfter: for w := 0; w < n; w++ { go func(){ results <- work() }() }
checkpoints.explanation: Sizing the buffer to n lets all n workers send their single result without waiting for a receiver, so none of them block (and none leak if main is slow to read). An unbuffered channel would force each worker to wait for main to receive.

codeLab.title: Concurrent map with bounded parallelism
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(nums []int, limit int) []int` that returns each n squared, computing them concurrently but with at most `limit` goroutines running at once. Use a buffered channel as a semaphore. Results must stay in input order.
hints: A buffered channel of size `limit` is a semaphore: send to acquire, receive to release.
Write each result into res[idx]; distinct indices mean no lock is needed.
Pass idx and val as arguments to avoid the loop-variable capture trap.

debuggingLab.title: Producer outpaces a too-small buffer
debuggingLab.symptom: The program hangs and crashes with a deadlock when sending the 3rd value.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: All sends happen before any receive, but the buffer holds only 2. The third send blocks waiting for a free slot, and since the receiving loop hasn't started (it's after the sends in the same goroutine), nothing ever drains the buffer — deadlock. The send and receive phases must overlap, or the buffer must be large enough.
commonMistakes: Doing all sends before any receives in a single goroutine with a too-small buffer.
Assuming a buffered channel can hold an unbounded number of sends.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Either size the buffer to hold all values, or move the receiving into a separate goroutine so sends and receives overlap.

theory.question: When does a send/receive on a buffered channel block?
theory.directAnswer: A send blocks only when the buffer is full; a receive blocks only when the buffer is empty. Otherwise both proceed immediately, with values delivered in FIFO order. The buffer decouples producer and consumer by up to its capacity.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The blocking rules for a channel with capacity n > 0.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To let producers and consumers run at different speeds with bounded slack.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Sends copy into the ring buffer when there's room; receives copy out from the front; full/empty conditions park the goroutine.

theory.whyImportant: Misjudging this causes deadlocks or hidden backpressure; it's a core interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A results channel sized to the worker count lets every worker send once without blocking.

followUps.question: How do len(ch) and cap(ch) behave?
followUps.answer: cap is the fixed buffer size; len is the current number of buffered, unreceived values.

followUps.question: Is FIFO guaranteed?
followUps.answer: Yes — buffered channels deliver values in send order.

theory.question: What are directional channel types and why use them in function signatures?
theory.directAnswer: chan<- T is send-only and <-chan T is receive-only. Using them in parameters documents and enforces a function's role — a producer can only send, a consumer can only receive (and can't close). A bidirectional chan T converts to either direction implicitly, but a directional type can't convert back.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Compile-time-restricted views of a channel value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To encode the data-flow contract in the type system and prevent misuse.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler rejects sends on a <-chan T or receives/closes on a chan<- T; at runtime it's the same channel.

theory.whyImportant: Directional types are pervasive in real pipeline APIs and signal strong API design.
theory.realWorldExample: func worker(jobs <-chan Job, results chan<- Result) makes the worker's role unambiguous.

followUps.question: Can a function close a <-chan T parameter?
followUps.answer: No — closing requires send capability; only a chan T or chan<- T can be closed (and by convention only the producer).

followUps.question: Why can't you convert <-chan T back to chan T?
followUps.answer: It would re-grant send rights you intentionally removed, defeating the restriction.

theory.question: How do cap(ch) and len(ch) differ for a buffered channel, and how do they change over time?
theory.directAnswer: cap(ch) is the fixed buffer size set at make(chan T, n) and never changes. len(ch) is the number of values currently sitting in the buffer, sent but not yet received; it rises on each send and falls on each receive, staying between 0 and cap. When len == cap the buffer is full and further sends block; when len == 0 it's empty and receives block.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two built-in queries against a channel's ring buffer: total capacity versus current occupancy.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To let code and monitoring reason about how full a buffer is without draining it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The runtime tracks the number of buffered elements in the hchan struct; len reads that counter and cap reads the fixed buffer length. Both are momentary snapshots and can change immediately in concurrent code.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two leads to wrong assumptions about blocking; exporting len/cap is also the standard way to observe buffer saturation.
theory.realWorldExample: A metrics exporter publishes len(ch)/cap(ch) as a gauge; a value pinned near 1.0 shows consumers can't keep up.

followUps.question: Is checking len(ch) before a send safe to avoid blocking?
followUps.answer: No — it races: another goroutine can fill the last slot between your len check and your send. Use a select with default for a truly non-blocking send.

followUps.question: What do len and cap return for an unbuffered channel?
followUps.answer: Both return 0, since an unbuffered channel has no buffer to hold values.

theory.question: How does the Go runtime implement a buffered channel differently from an unbuffered one, and what does that mean for a send?
theory.directAnswer: Both are the same hchan struct with a lock and sender/receiver wait queues, but a buffered channel also carries an n-element circular buffer. On an unbuffered channel a send always requires a waiting receiver and performs a direct handoff. On a buffered channel a send first tries to copy the value into a free buffer slot with no receiver present; only when the buffer is full does it park the sender on the wait queue.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The runtime data structure and send path behind chan T.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The buffer lets producers make progress without a receiver ready, decoupling the two goroutines up to n items.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A send acquires the channel lock, checks for a waiting receiver (direct copy), else copies into the ring buffer if there's room, else enqueues the sender's goroutine and parks it until a receive frees a slot.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding the mechanism explains exactly when goroutines park and why buffering improves throughput under rate mismatch.
theory.realWorldExample: A logging pipeline uses a small buffer so the hot path enqueues without parking, while a slower writer drains asynchronously.

followUps.question: Does buffering avoid the channel lock?
followUps.answer: No — every send and receive still takes the hchan lock; buffering only avoids the goroutine park/handoff when there is room.

followUps.question: Is the send-into-buffer path a copy or a reference?
followUps.answer: It copies the value into the buffer slot, so the value is snapshotted at send time.

scenario.question: A queue uses a large buffered channel 'so producers never block'. Latency looks fine in tests but the service OOMs under sustained overload. What's the design flaw?
scenario.directAnswer: An oversized buffer hides backpressure: producers keep enqueuing faster than consumers drain, and the buffer grows toward its capacity, holding more and more memory until the process OOMs. Buffering should absorb bursts, not mask a sustained rate mismatch. Bound the buffer to a realistic backlog and treat a full channel as a load-shedding signal (drop, reject, or slow the producer).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Backpressure masking via an excessive buffer.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A full buffer is the natural signal that consumers can't keep up; a huge buffer delays that signal until memory runs out.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Bounding capacity makes producers block or shed load, surfacing the imbalance before it exhausts memory.

scenario.whyImportant: Buffer-sizing mistakes are a common production OOM cause and a favorite scenario question.
scenario.realWorldExample: An ingestion service with a million-slot channel that fell behind during a traffic spike and crashed.

followUps.question: How do you shed load when the buffer is full?
followUps.answer: Use a non-blocking send (select with default) to drop or reject, and emit a metric so the overload is visible.

scenario.question: Your worker pool of 8 goroutines writes to a results channel created with make(chan Result) (unbuffered). Main collects results only after wg.Wait() returns. The program deadlocks. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The workers send on an unbuffered results channel, so each send blocks until main receives. But main is blocked in wg.Wait() and won't receive until every worker has finished — a circular wait that deadlocks. Fix it by sizing the results channel to the number of results workers produce (make(chan Result, len(jobs))) so every send lands in the buffer without a receiver, or by collecting results concurrently in a separate goroutine while workers run.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A fan-in deadlock caused by an unbuffered result channel plus a barrier before receiving.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An unbuffered send needs a live receiver; deferring all receives until after wg.Wait() removes that receiver during the send phase.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Buffering the channel to the total result count lets each worker send once and return, so wg.Wait() can complete and main then drains the buffer; alternatively, overlapping receive with the sends keeps a receiver present.

scenario.whyImportant: This exact ordering bug is one of the most common concurrency deadlocks and a frequent interview scenario.
scenario.realWorldExample: A batch aggregation job hung in production until the results channel was sized to the job count, letting workers finish before collection.

followUps.question: Why does closing the channel not fix the deadlock?
followUps.answer: Closing happens after wg.Wait(), which never returns because the workers are still blocked on their sends — the close is unreachable.

followUps.question: Which fix is preferable for very large result counts?
followUps.answer: Collecting in a concurrent goroutine, so you don't allocate a buffer proportional to the entire workload.

systemDesign.question: Design a bounded ingestion pipeline in Go for a high-throughput event service, using buffered and directional channels to absorb bursts while protecting against memory blowup.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Model the pipeline as stages connected by directional channels: an ingest stage sends on chan<- Event, worker stages take a <-chan Event and emit on a chan<- Result. Give each inter-stage channel a bounded buffer sized to a realistic burst (not unbounded), so short spikes are absorbed but sustained overload surfaces as backpressure. At the edge, use a non-blocking send (select with default) to shed load and increment a drop metric when the buffer is full, rather than growing memory. Cap concurrency per stage with a counting semaphore (buffered chan struct{}), and give each stage a single owner responsible for closing its output channel after its senders finish.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A staged producer/consumer pipeline with bounded buffered channels and directional types enforcing each stage's role.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To decouple stages that run at different speeds, absorb bursts, and keep memory bounded under sustained overload.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Bounded buffers provide slack between stages; a full buffer becomes the backpressure signal. Non-blocking sends at the edge convert overload into explicit load shedding. Semaphore channels cap in-flight work per stage, and clear channel ownership prevents send-on-closed panics.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It ties together every concept in the topic — buffer sizing, direction, backpressure, and semaphores — into a realistic, review-grade design.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A telemetry ingestion service that buffers each stage to a few thousand events, sheds load with a metric when saturated, and stays memory-stable during traffic spikes.

followUps.question: How would you observe whether the buffers are healthy?
followUps.answer: Export len(ch)/cap(ch) per stage as a saturation gauge; a value persistently near 1.0 means that stage is the bottleneck.

followUps.question: Who closes the channels and when?
followUps.answer: Each stage's coordinator closes its output channel exactly once, after a WaitGroup over that stage's senders completes, so downstream ranges terminate cleanly.

coding.question: Implement `func Worker(jobs <-chan int, results chan<- int)` that squares each job and sends the result, using directional channel types.
coding.thoughtProcess: The signature already encodes the roles: jobs is receive-only, results is send-only. Range over jobs (which ends when the producer closes it) and send each square on results. The directional types prevent accidentally closing jobs or receiving from results.
coding.lineByLine: jobs is <-chan int, so range jobs is the only legal use — it reads each job and stops when the producer closes the channel. results is chan<- int, so we may only send; the compiler would reject closing it or receiving from it, enforcing the worker's consumer/producer contract.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the n jobs received.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — no extra storage beyond the loop variable.

followUps.question: Who closes results when multiple Workers share it?
followUps.answer: Not the workers — a coordinator closes results once after a WaitGroup over all workers finishes.

followUps.question: What stops this worker from leaking?
followUps.answer: It returns when jobs is closed and drained; the producer must close jobs for the range to end.

coding.question: Implement `func TrySend(ch chan<- int, v int) bool` that sends v on a buffered channel if there is room, returning true on success and false immediately (without blocking) when the buffer is full.
coding.thoughtProcess: A plain send blocks when the buffer is full, which we must avoid. The idiomatic non-blocking send is a select with a default case: if the send can proceed it takes the send case and returns true; otherwise the default runs immediately and we return false. The chan<- int direction documents that this helper only produces.
coding.lineByLine: The select evaluates its cases: 'ch <- v' is ready only when the buffer has a free slot (or a receiver is waiting), in which case the value is sent and we return true. If the send would block, the default case is chosen immediately, so we return false without waiting. Because ch is chan<- int, the function can only send, matching the load-shedding intent.

followUps.question: How would you extend this to drop-and-count for load shedding?
followUps.answer: On the default branch, increment a dropped-events counter/metric before returning false so the shed load is observable.

followUps.question: Does this work on an unbuffered channel?
followUps.answer: Yes — the send case is ready only if a receiver is currently waiting; otherwise it returns false, effectively an offer-if-ready.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Encode data flow with directional types so each component's role is explicit. Size buffers deliberately: unbuffered for synchronization, small for burst absorption, worker-count for result fan-in.
productionDeepDive.performance: A buffer reduces goroutine parking when producer/consumer rates differ, improving throughput and tail latency; an oversized buffer wastes memory and hides backpressure that you actually want to observe.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Use a buffered channel as a counting semaphore to bound concurrency without a mutex. Keep one owner responsible for closing the channel after all senders finish.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Treat a full buffer as backpressure, not a problem to bury under more capacity; combine with non-blocking sends to shed load gracefully under overload.
productionDeepDive.observability: Export len(ch) versus cap(ch) as a saturation gauge; a buffer that stays near full means consumers can't keep up.
productionDeepDive.security: Bound buffers so a malicious or buggy producer can't drive unbounded memory growth; pair with rate limits at the edge.

caseStudies.problem: Spiky inbound load overwhelming downstream processing.
caseStudies.solution: A bounded buffered job channel absorbs bursts; a semaphore channel caps concurrency.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Buffer size trades memory and latency against the ability to absorb spikes.
caseStudies.lessons: Size buffers to a realistic backlog and surface saturation as a metric.

keyTakeaways: make(chan T, n) buffers up to n values; sends block only when full, receives only when empty, and order is FIFO.
cap(ch) is the buffer size; len(ch) is how many values are currently buffered and waiting.
Directional types — chan<- T (send-only) and <-chan T (receive-only) — encode and enforce producer/consumer roles at compile time.
Size buffers deliberately: oversized buffers hide backpressure and can cause OOMs; a full buffer is a load-shedding signal, not a bug to bury.
